title: Screen Time Needs a New Tune
author: Dan Meyer
summary: Dan Meyer argues that the edtech industry's problem is not screen time per se but instructional composition -- the melody teachers create by sequencing resources in a classroom. Just as a piece of music becomes boring when only one note is played repeatedly, students become disengaged when digital technology means only two notes: teacher explanation followed by silent independent screen work. Meyer draws on NYT reporting showing growing student and parent disenchantment with classroom devices, and contrasts monotonous single-mode edtech with a whiteboard routine that interleaves teacher questions, student responses, and explanations across multiple instruments. In his own teaching example using a digital card sort, students moved in and out of laptops every few minutes -- laptops became objects passed between students for conversation, creating a chord of multiple simultaneous learning modalities. His prescription: edtech must earn its place in the melody by delivering unique value no analog substitute could match, and teachers must compose richer, more varied sequences that treat screens as one instrument among many.
points: * Teaching is the work of composition: teachers arrange resources -- technology, whiteboards, paper, discussion, physical space -- into learning experiences, and the sequence matters as much as the tools. * Digital technology frequently produces as monotonous a melody as a teacher speaking endlessly at a blackboard -- two notes (teacher explanation then screen work) instead of a varied, engaging sequence. * Students' relationship to screens has shifted post-pandemic: what once generated dopamine now generates glazed disengagement, even amid rapturous media coverage of classroom AI. * Because computers incur heavy switching costs (login time, log-out risk), edtech must bring more value to an experience than any analog substitute -- otherwise the switching cost alone argues against it. * Meyer's practical example: a digital card sort that instantly identified the class's hardest problem was worth the screen time precisely because no paper equivalent could match that analytical speed.
quotes: In many classrooms, students find the melody pretty dull -- regardless of the teacher's use of education technology.
Digital technology frequently produces as monotonous a melody as a teacher speaking endlessly in front of a blackboard.
These devices are some of humanity's most incredible achievements, but when students use them in schools they often hear only two notes -- teacher explanation and screens.
Education technology needs to bring more value to a learning experience than any analog substitute.
'How much screen time is too much?' is an important question, but just one of many. We should also wonder what students do with their time on screens and what purpose that work serves.

We should wonder how we can play a more interesting melody with computers in class, kids switching in and out of them as easily as switching between people in a conversation, between pages in a book, between instruments in a symphony called learning.
